source.title: @GrokSet: multi-party Human-LLM Interactions in Social Media
source.authors: Matteo Migliarini; Berat Ercevik; Oluwagbemike Olowe; Saira Fatima; Sarah A. Zhao; Minh Le; Vasu Sharma; Ashwinee Panda

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes real-world Grok responses to user interactions and reports safety failures linked to persona adoption and tone mirroring. This bears on the bypass claim, using observational and qualitative methods rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The safety results are Detoxify counts and qualitative findings about the user prompts preceding flagged replies. The paper does not test fine-tuning, KL by response position, compliant-token prefilling, suffix attacks, decoding changes, safety-related weight localization, or training to deepen safety. Engagement and topic results do not bear on the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the 'shallow alignment' label from Qi et al. (2024), but none of its results bear on any version. It reports Detoxify counts of toxic or profane Grok replies on X, plus a qualitative review of what users wrote before those replies. None of this measures harmful-request compliance after fine-tuning (V1, V2), per-position KL (V3), or prefill, suffix or decoding bypass of refusal (V4). It also does not test weight localization (V5), causes of shallowness (V6) or deepening training (V7). Persona and tone-mirroring prompts eliciting profanity are a related but different construct: instruction-following into an offensive style, not getting past a refusal's opening. They are recorded under fits_no_version. The one harmful-request observation (r10) comes from Detoxify-flagged cases only, so it cannot show whether Grok complies with harmful requests.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say Grok generally maintains robust safety filters, with toxic replies a fringe 0.09%. Its 'shallow' alignment (their term, citing Qi et al.) is bypassed through persona adoption and tone mirroring rather than complex jailbreaks. They found no compliance with direct adversarial prompts in flagged cases. They call the toxicity rate a conservative lower bound because of survivorship bias from platform moderation.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes an in-the-wild corpus of Grok conversations and applies Detoxify plus manual review; it does not reproduce a fine-tuning or token-position experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: In deployed Grok on X, 366 replies (0.09%) exceeded Detoxify thresholds. These were mostly obscene, toxic, insult and sexual-explicit replies; threats, identity attacks and severe toxicity were zero. Manual review attributes them mainly to user persona requests and hostile tone that Grok mirrored.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deployed aligned LLMs in public multi-party settings produce offensive-style outputs when users request personas or use hostile register (instruction-following overriding style or toxicity norms), at low base rates.

record.problems: For the safety findings, the study uses automated toxicity labels and qualitative review rather than a controlled intervention or refusal-rate evaluation. The authors note survivorship bias, because severe failures may have been removed before collection, and potential bias from automated labeling tools. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the safety counts.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, or refusal-rate measurement on harmful requests.
No analysis of data or objective causes.

record.verdict_notes: Using 'shallow alignment' as a label does not make this a test of the token-depth claim; no row measures refusal, its opening tokens, or harmful-request compliance. The reader's V4 labels are removed. The record also omits the Sexual Explicit count (36) from Table 3.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and refusal after fine-tuning.
Benign-data fine-tuning and resulting harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
No controlled test of compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes; no systematic test of direct harmful-request compliance.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training to deepen safety and whether the resulting safety holds up.

rows.subject: Grok
rows.operation_detail: Counted assistant replies exceeding Detoxify toxicity thresholds in the collected conversations.
rows.note: The authors describe these as rare safety failures; the count does not measure refusal rates for a controlled prompt set.
rows.check: A toxicity rate (366 flagged replies, 0.09%) in an uncontrolled corpus with no baseline or refusal measure. It does not measure V4's prefill, suffix or decoding bypass. 'Partial' has no referent.

rows.subject: Grok
rows.operation_detail: Manually reviewed Detoxify-flagged cases for conversational antecedents to safety failures.
rows.measure: Qualitative finding about safety failures following persona instructions
rows.value: The authors report that users instructed the model to adopt a fictional character and that it prioritized the character instruction over standard refusal protocols.
rows.note: The report concerns observed cases in the corpus, not a controlled prompt experiment.
rows.check: A qualitative antecedent finding with no frequency. A persona instruction producing profanity is not a prefill, suffix or decoding bypass of refusal, so it does not test V4.

rows.subject: Grok
rows.operation_detail: Manually reviewed Detoxify-flagged cases for conversational antecedents to safety failures.
rows.measure: Qualitative finding about safety failures following hostile or profane user language
rows.value: The authors report that Grok occasionally mirrored users’ aggressive slang or profanity, which they describe as slipping past safety alignment.
rows.note: The authors describe this pattern as occasional; no frequency for this antecedent is given.
rows.check: A qualitative finding ('occasionally' mirrors hostile register) with no frequency. It shows style mimicry, not refusal bypass via the opening tokens.

rows.subject: Grok
rows.operation_detail: Qualitatively inspected flagged safety-failure cases for direct adversarial-prompt compliance.

conditions.value: Direct adversarial prompts, for example requests for bomb-building instructions

rows.measure: Whether an instance of compliance was identified
rows.value: The authors report that their qualitative inspection did not reveal an instance.
rows.note: This is a qualitative finding from flagged cases, not a systematic test of direct adversarial prompts.
rows.check: Only Detoxify-flagged replies were inspected. Compliance with a bomb-building request would not necessarily be flagged by a toxicity classifier, so this cannot show presence or absence of harmful compliance.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report occasional mirroring of hostile or profane user language as a safety failure (r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Collected replies and the reviewed flagged cases
reader_labels.reason: The authors describe toxicity as rare (0.09% of responses) and report no direct adversarial-prompt compliance instance in their qualitative review; these findings do not establish broad or systematic bypass of harmful-request refusals (r1, r10).
